description: Test your knowledge of PA MG1 | Male Genital Tract testicular tumors classification, risk factors, and pathogenesis.

cards.text: What are the three broad categories of testicular tumors based on cell of origin?
cards.answer: Germ cell tumors (95% of cases, from pluripotent germ cells), sex cord-stromal tumors (from Sertoli or Leydig cells), and lymphoma (from B lymphocytes).

tip.tip: Remember 'GSL': Germ cell, Sex cord-stromal, Lymphoma

cards.text: What percentage of GCTs are seminoma, and why is this clinically important?
cards.answer: Seminoma comprises ~55% of GCTs and is exquisitely radiosensitive, whereas NSGCTs (~45%) require cisplatin-based chemotherapy — treatment differs fundamentally.

tip.tip: Seminoma > 50% of GCTs; "radiosensitive" is its defining feature

cards.text: Describe GCNIS (germ cell neoplasia in situ) and name its two hallmark features.
cards.answer: GCNIS is a precursor lesion of atypical large cells lining seminiferous tubules; it expresses OCT3/4 and PLAP (embryonic markers) and harbors isochromosome 12p in ~80% of cases.

tip.tip: GCNIS = OCT3/4 + PLAP + i(12p) = precursor to all invasive GCTs

cards.text: What is isochromosome 12p and which genes on 12p promote GCT progression?
cards.answer: i(12p) is duplication of the 12p short arm (with loss of 12q); it contains oncogenes KRAS, CCND2, NANOG, and DAD-R that drive pluripotency and cell survival in ~80% of GCTs.

tip.tip: 12p doubled = 2 copies of growth-promoting genes; this is the GCT's genetic hallmark

cards.text: What is the relationship between cryptorchidism and testicular GCT risk?
cards.answer: Cryptorchidism confers 3–5-fold increased risk in the undescended testis and 2-fold risk in the contralateral testis; even after successful orchiopexy, residual risk persists because cryptorchidism is a marker of testicular dysgenesis, not just mechanical.

tip.tip: Undescended testis: 3–5×risk; opposite side: 2×risk — risk persists after fix

cards.text: Name four major risk factors for testicular GCT beyond cryptorchidism.
cards.answer: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY), testicular dysgenesis syndrome, prior contralateral GCT (2–3% lifetime risk), and strong family history (8–10-fold risk in first-degree relatives).

tip.tip: K-D-C-F: Klinefelter, Dysgenesis, Contralateral, Family history

cards.text: How does the differentiation status of GCNIS determine whether a tumor becomes seminoma or NSGCT?
cards.answer: Undifferentiated GCNIS → seminoma; totipotent (embryonic) GCNIS → embryonal carcinoma and other NSGCTs. The lineage of differentiation determines the final histological type.

tip.tip: Less differentiated = seminoma (most primitive); more embryonic = embryonal CA (most aggressive NSGCT)

cards.text: What are the three most common NSGCTs and their key diagnostic markers?
cards.answer: Embryonal carcinoma (most aggressive), yolk sac tumor (AFP-positive, most common in infants), and choriocarcinoma (β-hCG-positive, prone to hemorrhage); mixed GCTs are the most common NSGCT overall (~50%).
